commons:441106.summary: Beneath the Latin text of the psalm, Christ, with a cross-nimbus and a red cloak, stands in the dress of a soldier holding a book and a cross-staff whose point he drives down on the beasts at his feet: a serpent-like dragon and a lion. An angel at the left raises its hands in wonder and a hand reaches from the heavens at the upper right. The miniature reads the psalm as a prophecy of Christ's victory over evil.
facts: The Stuttgart Psalter (Cod. Bibl. fol. 23) was made around 820 at Saint-Germain-des-Prés in Paris and contains 316 illustrations of the Psalms; the 'fol23' in the file name is the manuscript's shelfmark, not the folio.
This miniature illustrates Psalm 91 (90):13 on folio 107v: 'super aspidem et basiliscum ambulabis et conculcabis leonem et draconem'.
The verse was sung daily at Compline and in the Roman Good Friday liturgy, which helped make the image of Christ trampling the beasts a symbol of his triumph over Satan.

cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-15-christ.summary: In this lower drawing on the page Christ appears twice: as the bearded Christ-Logos holding a scroll among angels in the heavens, and, below at the left, as the beardless Christ trampling Hades and drawing Adam and Eve out of the pit. The scene illustrates the verse 'thou wilt not leave my soul in hell', which the apostles read as a prophecy of the Resurrection (Acts 2:27). It is an early Western example of the Descent into Hell.
facts: The Utrecht Psalter illustrates every psalm and canticle with a lively pen drawing — 166 in all — that translates the words of the text, often literally, into images; in these the Lord of the psalms is regularly shown as the youthful Christ-Logos.
Its text is written in rustic capitals, an archaic script that once led scholars to date the manuscript to the 6th century; the drawings are now recognised as Carolingian.
cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-15-christ.notes: The figure of the Lord is identified as Christ (the Christ-Logos) following the commentary of the Utrecht University Library's annotated edition, which describes the psalter's consistent practice of drawing the God of the psalms as the youthful Christ. The image is a crop of the drawing from the library's IIIF image server. This folio carries two drawings; the crop shows the one for this text.

cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-113-chris.summary: A walled city with idols on its turrets stands for Egypt, out of which Moses leads the Israelites, striking the rock so that water gushes out. Above Moses the beardless Christ-Logos with a book, in a mandorla among angels, blesses a group bearing the ark of the covenant. Christ is shown as the Lord of the Exodus, in the lower drawing of folio 66r.

cur:monumental-classe-arch-christ-tetram.summary: In a round medallion at the summit of the triumphal arch, a bearded Christ raises his right hand in blessing and holds a jewelled book in his left. He floats in a sea of red and blue clouds, flanked by the winged symbols of the evangelists, here the man of Matthew and the lion of Mark. The image crowns the arch above the sixth-century apse with its great jewelled cross of the Transfiguration.
facts: The four winged creatures around Christ are the symbols of the evangelists: eagle (John), man (Matthew), lion (Mark) and calf (Luke).
Below them, twelve lambs, symbols of the apostles, issue from the jewelled cities of Jerusalem and Bethlehem.
The church was consecrated on 9 May 549 by Bishop Maximian, but the arch mosaics belong to later campaigns of decoration.

met:468482.summary: This marble head of a mature man with a full, curling beard and long hair falling to the shoulders was carved in the Roman manner and, according to the Metropolitan Museum, later transformed; it may represent Zeus, or Christ, or a Zeus image reworked as Christ. It vividly illustrates how the bearded, majestic image of Christ drew on the long tradition of classical images of the father of the gods.
facts: The Met dates the head to the 3rd or 4th century with a later transformation, and titles it 'Head of Christ or Zeus', leaving the identification open.
The bearded, long-haired type of Christ that became standard from the late 4th century onward owes much to classical images of Zeus and of philosophers.
met:468482.notes: Identification as Christ is uncertain (the museum itself hedges). Kept because the Met lists 'Christ' as a subject, but an editor may prefer to exclude it.
